lesson_1.title: Backtracking Architecture: The Power Set
task: Implement a backtracking architecture to generate the power set of an array of size N.
Phase 1: Setup & Base Case
Define `power_set(arr)` initializing a `results` array and a `backtrack(start_index, current_path)` helper function. The base case unconditionally appends a deep copy of `current_path` to `results`.
Phase 2: Iteration & Selection
Iterate `i` from `start_index` to the end of `arr`. Append `arr[i]` to `current_path` to represent element selection.
Phase 3: Recursive Descent
Invoke `backtrack(i + 1, current_path)` to explore the decision tree.
Phase 4: Backtracking
Upon return, pop the last element from `current_path` to revert state for subsequent iterations.

lesson_1.title: Subsets with a Target Sum
task: Adapt the backtracking architecture to identify subsets of an array of size N that sum to a specified target.
Instructions:
1. Define `target_subsets(arr, target)` and a `backtrack(start_index, current_path, current_sum)` helper.
2. Base Case: If `current_sum == target`, append a copy of `current_path` to the results.
3. Pruning Condition: If `current_sum > target`, terminate the branch immediately (`return`).
4. Iterate `i` from `start_index` to the array's end, appending `arr[i]` to `current_path`.
5. Recursion: Invoke `backtrack(i + 1, current_path, current_sum + arr[i])`.
6. Backtrack: Pop the last element from the path.

lesson_1.title: Generating Combinations
task: Generate all unique combinations of size `k` chosen from the mathematical range 1 to `N`.
Instructions:
1. Define `combine(n, k)` and a `backtrack(start, path)` helper.
2. Base Case: If `len(path) == k`, append a deep copy of the path to results and return.
3. Iterate `i` from `start` to `n + 1`.
4. Select: Append `i` to the path.
5. Recurse: Call `backtrack(i + 1, path)`.
6. Backtrack: Pop the element from the path.

lesson_1.title: Combinations with Repetition
task: Modify the combination generator to allow unbounded repetition of elements from an array of size N to reach a specific target.
Instructions:
1. Define `combine_repeat(arr, target)`.
2. Base Case: If `sum == target`, append the path and return. If `sum > target`, return to prune the branch.
3. Iterate `i` from `start_index` to the end. Select `arr[i]`.
4. Recurse: Invoke `backtrack(i, path, new_sum)`. Passing `i` rather than `i + 1` permits element reuse.
5. Backtrack: Pop the element.

lesson_1.title: Letter Combinations (Phone Keypad)
task: Compute all possible letter combinations representing a given string of N digits, mapped via a standard telephone keypad.
Instructions:
1. Define `phone_letters(digits)`. If `digits` is empty, return `[]`. Initialize a dictionary mapping digits to characters.
2. Define `backtrack(index, path)`.
3. Base Case: If `index == len(digits)`, append the joined `path` string to results and return.
4. Retrieve the character set for the current digit.
5. Iterate over each character. Append the character, recurse to `index + 1`, and backtrack.

lesson_2.title: Permutations Architecture
task: Implement a backtracking algorithm to generate all permutations of an array of size N. Permutations require sequence ordering tracking.
Phase 1: Base Case
Define `permute(arr)` and `backtrack(path, used)`. Base Case: If `len(path) == len(arr)`, append a copy of the path to results and return.
Phase 2: State Tracking & Iteration
Iterate `i` from 0 to the end of the array. If `arr[i]` exists in the `used` set, `continue` to bypass.
Phase 3: Selection, Recursion, Reversion
Append `arr[i]` to `path` and add it to `used`. Recurse via `backtrack(path, used)`. Backtrack by removing `arr[i]` from both structures.

lesson_2.title: Permutations with Duplicates
task: Generate unique permutations for an array of size N containing duplicate elements, implementing structural pruning to prevent duplicate branch evaluation.
Instructions:
1. Define `permute_unique(arr)`. Sort the array to group identical elements.
2. Modify the `used` tracker to store array indices rather than values.
3. Iterate `i` from 0 to the end. Skip if `i` is in `used`.
4. Pruning Condition: If `i > 0`, `arr[i] == arr[i-1]`, and `(i - 1)` is not in `used`, `continue` to bypass redundant branches.
5. Execute standard selection, recursion, and backtracking operations.

lesson_2.title: Word Scrambler
task: Apply permutation logic to generate all unique anagrams of a given string of length N.
Instructions:
1. Define `scramble_word(word)`. Cast the string to a character array.
2. Initialize a `used` index set and an empty `path` tracking structure.
3. Base Case: If the path length matches the word length, join the characters and append to results.
4. Iterate over indices `i`. Bypass if `i` is in `used`.
5. Append `chars[i]`, recurse, and backtrack.

lesson_2.title: Restricted Permutations
task: Implement constrained permutations on a string of length N by introducing an early-termination pruning rule.
Instructions:
1. Define `safe_scramble(word)` incorporating standard permutation architecture.
2. Pruning Condition: Immediately following character selection, evaluate constraints.
3. If `len(path) == 1` and `path[0] == 'Z'`, immediately execute the backtrack removal operation and `continue` to prune the branch.

lesson_2.title: Counting Arrangements (No Lists)
task: Optimize memory allocation by computing the total count of permutations for an array of size N without storing the sequences.
Instructions:
1. Define `count_permutations(arr)`. Initialize a local `count` variable.
2. In the `backtrack(path, used)` helper, modify the base case: rather than appending to a matrix, increment `count` and return.
3. Implement standard permutation traversal logic.
4. Return the final scalar `count`.

lesson_3.title: Maze Solver: The Rules of the Grid
task: Establish boundary and obstacle evaluation rules for a 2D matrix traversal. Let N represent rows and M represent columns. (0: empty, 1: wall, 9: target).
Phase 1: Boundary Verification
Define `solve_maze(grid)` and a recursive `explore(row, col)` helper. Rule 1: If `row` or `col` exceed the N x M boundaries (`< 0` or `>= length`), return `False`.
Phase 2: Obstacle Verification
Rule 2: If `grid[row][col] == 1`, return `False`.
Phase 3: Target Verification
Rule 3: If `grid[row][col] == 9`, return `True`.

lesson_3.title: Maze Solver: Moving Right and Down
task: Implement constrained directional traversal (Right and Down only) through an N x M matrix to locate a target.
Instructions:
1. Define `maze_simple(grid)` with the `explore(row, col)` helper.
2. Implement boundary, wall, and target base cases.
3. Recursive Descent: If `explore(row + 1, col)` evaluates to `True`, cascade `True` upwards.
4. If downward traversal fails, evaluate rightward traversal: `explore(row, col + 1)`.
5. If all evaluated directions terminate in failure, return `False`.

lesson_3.title: Maze Solver: All 4 Directions (Avoiding Cycles)
task: Implement full 4-directional matrix traversal. Introduce state tracking to prevent infinite cyclical evaluation within the N x M grid.
Phase 1: State Initialization
Initialize a `visited` set within the primary function scope.
Phase 2: Position Selection
Add a traversal rule: If `(row, col)` exists in `visited`, return `False`. Otherwise, append the coordinate to `visited`.
Phase 3: Multi-directional Recursion
Evaluate `row+1`, `row-1`, `col+1`, and `col-1` sequentially. Return `True` upon any successful evaluation.
Phase 4: State Reversion
Upon exhausting all directions, remove `(row, col)` from `visited` and return `False`.

lesson_3.title: Maze Solver: Tracking the Path
task: Record the successful traversal sequence through an N x M matrix to reach a defined target.
Instructions:
1. Define `maze_path(grid)` allocating a `path` sequence array and a `visited` set.
2. Append current `[row, col]` coordinates to `path` upon validation.
3. Recursively evaluate all 4 directions. If a recursive call returns `True`, immediately cascade `True` upwards without path modification.
4. If all directions fail, execute backtracking by popping the terminal coordinate from `path`, removing it from `visited`, and returning `False`.

lesson_3.title: Maze Solver: Counting All Paths
task: Calculate the aggregate sum of all valid traversal paths through an N x M matrix to the target.
Instructions:
1. Define `count_maze_paths(grid)` with a zero-initialized `count` variable.
2. Modify the target base case: If `grid[row][col] == 9`, increment `count`, remove the coordinate from `visited` to enable alternate path discovery, and return.
3. Recursively evaluate all 4 directions independently, omitting early-termination `return True` cascades.
4. Post-evaluation, remove `(row, col)` from `visited` to complete state reversion.

lesson_4.title: DP Matrix: Coin Change Initialization
task: Initialize a structured 2D dynamic programming matrix for the Coin Change algorithm. Let N equal the number of available coin denominations, and M equal the target amount.
Instructions:
1. Define `init_coin_dp(coins, amount)`.
2. Allocate an (N + 1) by (M + 1) dimensional nested array.
3. Populate all indices with `99999` to denote an uncalculated maximal state.
4. Base Case Initialization: Iterate over all rows, setting index `[i][0] = 0` to denote zero coins required for a zero amount target.
5. Return the initialized matrix.

lesson_4.title: DP Matrix: Filling Coin Change
task: Execute DP tabulation to populate the N x M Coin Change matrix by evaluating inclusion versus exclusion states.
Instructions:
1. Define `coin_change(coins, amount)` and initialize the matrix as specified previously.
2. Iterate `i` across rows (1 to N + 1) and `j` across columns (1 to M + 1).
3. Extract the current denomination: `coin = coins[i-1]`.
4. Tabulation Logic: If `coin <= j`, update the current cell to the minimum of either the excluded state (`dp[i-1][j]`) or the included state shifted by the denomination (`1 + dp[i][j - coin]`).
5. If the constraint fails, directly inherit the excluded state.
6. Return `dp[-1][-1]`, defaulting to `-1` if the state remains `99999`.

lesson_4.title: DP Matrix: Knapsack Initialization
task: Initialize the tabulation matrix for the 0/1 Knapsack optimization algorithm. Let N equal the item count, and M equal the maximum weight capacity.
Instructions:
1. Define `init_knapsack(weights, values, max_weight)`.
2. Allocate an (N + 1) by (M + 1) dimensional nested array.
3. Populate all indices with `0`, representing the baseline zero-value state.
4. Return the initialized matrix.

lesson_4.title: DP Matrix: Filling the Knapsack
task: Execute DP tabulation to optimize the 0/1 Knapsack N x M matrix by evaluating item value retention against weight capacities.
Instructions:
1. Define `knapsack(weights, values, max_weight)`.
2. Iterate `i` across items (1 to N + 1) and `w` across capacities (1 to M + 1).
3. Tabulation Logic: If `weights[i-1] <= w`, calculate the maximum of the excluded state (`dp[i-1][w]`) versus the included state (`values[i-1] + dp[i-1][w - weights[i-1]]`).
4. If the weight constraint fails, directly inherit the excluded state.
5. Return the terminal optimal value located at `dp[-1][-1]`.

lesson_4.title: DP Matrix: Longest Common Subsequence
task: Given two words, find the length of the longest sequence of letters they share in the same order (they don't have to be consecutive!).
Instructions:
1. Define `lcs(word1, word2)`. Create a DP matrix sized (len(word1) + 1) by (len(word2) + 1), filled with `0`s.
2. Iterate `r` from 1 to the end of rows, and `c` from 1 to the end of columns.
3. Match Check: If `word1[r-1] == word2[c-1]`, they share a letter! Set `dp[r][c] = 1 + dp[r-1][c-1]` (diagonal top-left).
4. Mismatch Check: If they don't match, carry forward the best previous score. Set `dp[r][c]` to the maximum of `dp[r-1][c]` (top) or `dp[r][c-1]` (left).
5. Return `dp[-1][-1]`, which holds the final length.

optimizations.title: Optimization Challenge: Memoizing the Matrix
task: Implement top-down Dynamic Programming via recursion and a memoization dictionary to optimize processing overhead.
Optimization Guidelines:
1. Define `knapsack_memo(weights, values, capacity, index, memo)`. Default `memo` to `{}`.
2. Base Case Verification: Return `0` if `index < 0` or `capacity == 0`.
3. Cache Verification: If the `(index, capacity)` state exists in `memo`, return the cached integer.
4. Constraint Evaluation: If `weights[index] > capacity`, recurse to `index - 1` and cache the result.
5. Optimal Selection: Compute both excluded (`index - 1`) and included (value addition with reduced capacity) recursive branches. Cache and return the maximum.

optimizations.title: Optimization Challenge: 1D Coin Change
task: A 2D matrix wastes a lot of memory. Because Coin Change only looks back at smaller amounts in the current row, we can compress the whole matrix into a single 1D Array!
Optimization Guidelines:
1. Define `coin_change_1d(coins, amount)`.
2. Create a single 1D array called `dp` sized `amount + 1`, filled with `99999`. Set `dp[0] = 0`.
3. Loop `coin` through the `coins` list.
4. Inside that, loop `a` (amount) FORWARD from `coin` up to `amount + 1`.
5. State Update: Set `dp[a]` to the minimum of its current value (`dp[a]`) OR `1 + dp[a - coin]`.
6. Return `dp[-1]` (return `-1` if it is still `99999`).
